text: Given an m by n grid of non-negative numbers, find a path from top-left to bottom-right, moving only right or down, that minimizes the sum of numbers along the path.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — only right and down, all values non-negative, and I return the minimum total, not the path itself?
Correct — just the minimum sum, grid up to two hundred by two hundred.
Let me run through an example. One, three, one; one, five, one; four, two, one — the path one, three, one, one, one sums to seven, which is minimal.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. This problem reminds me of a two-D grid DP — the path-counting kind, but optimizing instead of counting. Same skeleton: I reach cell i, j from above or from the left, but I take the cheaper predecessor. So dp of i, j is grid of i, j plus the min of the cell above and the cell to the left. The first row and column are prefix sums, not ones, since there's a single path along an edge but the cost accumulates.

Here's the plan. One: the start is just its own cost. Two: fill the first row and first column with prefix sums. Three: every other cell is its own cost plus the cheaper of up and left; return the bottom-right. One thing worth flagging — the only change from the path-counting version is swapping plus for min, plus the cell cost, and the boundary becomes prefix sums instead of all ones. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it, and the order n space version.

The two-D version: start cell, two prefix-sum loops for the edges, then min of up and left plus the cell cost. And the order n space rolling version: one row, seeded with the first row's prefix sums. Both are order m times n time. One thing worth flagging — in the rolling version, each new row starts with dp of zero plus-equals grid of i, zero, because the first column has no left neighbor; its only predecessor is the value above, which dp of zero still holds.

Let's dry-run the table on the example — expected seven. The cell that matters is the corner: dp two, two is its own cost one, plus the min of up six and left eight, so one plus six, seven. That's the path one, three, one, one, one. Correct. Corner cases: a single cell returns its own value, and a single row or column is just the prefix sum.

Time is order m times n, space order m times n, or order n with the rolling row. Oh, one more thing — this is the same grid skeleton again: counting paths uses plus, obstacles add a zero rule, and here I minimize with min. Swap the aggregate, keep the depends-on-up-and-left bones. A greedy always-step-to-the-smaller-cell would fail — on this very example it goes down, down, and ends at nine. Min compares accumulated costs, not single cells, which is why it's DP.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw it as the path-counting grid with plus swapped for min, and prefix-sum boundaries. You compressed to one row with the first-column fix. And you contrasted min of accumulated cost with a naive greedy. Good work.
